Sarah Guo on being contrarian:

"Unlike my good friends at Founders Fund, I don't have an instinct to be contrarian.

But it is so fundamental to decide what you think and not worry too much about what other people think. 

And 'other people' is like the dominant narratives of the period, or even what different players in the ecosystem that are really important, declare one way or another. 

I think you just need to find the truth.

If you find the truth and it's wrongly priced and you hold onto that, you're in a good position. 

You want asymmetric information, and then the confidence to hold the opinion when other people haven't come around to it yet.

I think a lot about how to make sure we have the information that is better than other people's, and then protect ourselves from noise."

Growth doesn't just solve a startup's problems in the sense of making them go away. It solves them like you solve a math problem. For example, it can design your product for you: start with something minimal, then add whatever will make you grow.

Over the summer, we have been sprinting on safety priorities; it's more important than ever for capabilities and safeguards to advance together. We have more to do but have made a lot of progress. We are also going to be launching our next model soon.

There is an obvious tension here: on one hand, Astra is very good and we are excited to see what people will build with it. We are proud of our work.

On the other hand, we are clearly in a phase of development where we believe caution is warranted, and we are pacing our progress to ensure that we can meet the safety standards required by new capability levels.

Astra has been done training for a while now and is a significant step forward in both capabilities and alignment. For the models after that, we have been slowing things as needed to ensure that we can do sufficient work on safety and alignment.

AI is getting extremely capable; no one fully understands the consequences of this. Managing the transition to a world with abundant and powerful AI to optimize for safety and benefits to people should be one of the highest priorities in the world. It is our highest priority at OpenAI.

We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time, and it is still discordant for us. We know it is much more discordant for other people. And yet, we believe strongly that the world needs to understand where AI is going and how models perform in the real world. More importantly, we believe the world will need aligned AI to manage the future phases of this transition.

An iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.

So we hope you enjoy our new model, and we hope the world continues to take what’s happening in AI extremely seriously.

Global liquidity grows at roughly 8% a year. Sounds great right? Except that liquidity isn't organic growth... it's money being created to service the world's enormous debts. And every new dollar created makes the ones you already hold worth less.

Add 3% inflation and you’re looking at an 11% hurdle rate just to break even. If your investments aren’t generating at LEAST 11% a year, you're not making money. This is why so many people feel like they can't get ahead... in real terms, they aren't.

I've spent the best part of three decades trying to work out why the economy stopped working for ordinary people. Over time it all distilled into one framework: The Everything Code.

Debasement sits at the heart of it...  and the 11% hurdle rate is the crux of the whole thing. Once you understand it, you'll understand how to unfuck your future.

For the first time, all of this thinking is in one place. My book, The Everything Code, comes out Nov 3rd... everything I've learned about how the system works, and how to end up on the right side of it, in plain English, for the people the economy stopped working for.

Pre-orders are now open. I'll drop the link below.

Debasement sits at the heart of it...  and the 11% hurdle rate is the crux of the whole thing. Once you understand it, you'll understand how to unfuck your future.

@friedberg:

“Treat scientists like the rock stars that they should be. Otherwise, you're going to lose them?”

@ericweinstein:

“When you have administrator types come in and say, ‘What we need is KPIs. I'm data-driven. I want to know what the translation is.’

Do you even know what ROI is, or is it just what you can measure?

You want these people on retainer, so whenever you have a real problem, you call up the most terrifying intellects you can imagine, and we can get to work and we can solve your problems.

If you tell me, ‘You should work on this because this thing is what drives the ROI,’ my feeling is, do you just not understand science?

Do you imagine that your technology mindset is the same thing as my scientific mindset? You want to get paid. I’ve spent a lot of time in Silicon Valley. I'm not nearly as interested in having a new McLaren as whether my name is going to be discussed 10,000 years from now if humans are still around.

We're in some sort of crazy world in which people who have radical ideas can't do the radical ideas inside of the institutions.

When people say something different, do you force them back into this consensus?

Well, that's what p*ssy nations do. And we have become a p*ssy nation when it comes to science.”

TLDR 

- DeFi/private-credit protocol that finances AI data centres and GPUs.

- Stablecoin holders provide capital → https://t.co/WXWhPdMSPl lends it to GPU infrastructure companies. Think “on-chain bank for GPU financing.”

The Opportunity

- AI infrastructure needs trillions of dollars of financing.

- Banks aren’t great at bespoke GPU-backed loans.
Apollo/Blackstone/etc. generally target huge $250M–$1B+ deals.

- https://t.co/WXWhPdMSPl targets the underserved middle market: loans up to ~$250M.

- https://t.co/WXWhPdMSPl estimates this market could need ~$2T financing.

How It Works

- Deposit stablecoins → receive USDai.

- Stake USDai → sUSDai.

- https://t.co/WXWhPdMSPl lends the money to GPU/data-centre operators.

- Borrowers pay interest + origination fees. sUSDai holders receive most of the interest.

- Protocol/DAO keeps fees + net interest margin (NIM).

Current Traction

- ~$430M TVL. ~$265M loans deployed. ~$230M additional signed term sheets. ~$30M annualized revenue attributable to DAO.

- sUSDai yield ≈ 7.7%, potentially >10% as more capital gets deployed.

How they protect against GPU depreciation/defaults

- Maximum 80% LTV.

- Loans amortize over ~3 years → principal gets paid down as GPUs depreciate. 

- GPU collateral + revenue contracts placed in bankruptcy-remote SPVs.

- https://t.co/WXWhPdMSPl gets first claim on GPUs/cash flows after default.

- Diversification across borrowers and GPU models.

- Barker insurance is intended to cover remaining losses after collateral recovery.

Biggest bottleneck
- Not enough capital rather than not enough borrowers.

- TVL has fallen ~37% this year.

- They need more stablecoin deposits to fund the loan pipeline.

- Potential sources: DeFi integrations, exchanges/fintechs and institutions.

Growth target

- Targeting $1B annual loan originations by EOY 2026.

- Arete’s 2027 base case: $2.5B annual originations.

- Estimated ~$68.8M annual revenue by end-2027.

CHIP token

- CHIP is essentially the speculative investment on https://t.co/WXWhPdMSPl’s growth.

- Major problem: CHIP currently has no strong structural value accrual.

- https://t.co/WXWhPdMSPl can make lots of money without CHIP necessarily benefiting.

- Arete expects future buybacks/burns/staking similar to HYPE/VVV.

This potential tokenomics change is a major part of their bull thesis.

Thesis in one line

AI boom → massive GPU financing demand → https://t.co/WXWhPdMSPl fills underserved lending gap → loan book/revenue grows → CHIP gets value accrual → CHIP potentially rerates.

Most important things to watch

- Can https://t.co/WXWhPdMSPl grow TVL/capital?

- Can it originate loans without sacrificing underwriting quality?

- Do defaults remain low?

- Does the claimed insurance protection work in practice?

- Does CHIP actually receive protocol economics? ← probably the biggest one.
